extra.message: Unsigned session cookies allow trivial session forgery — Complete authentication bypass; attacker impersonates any user including admin by crafting a cookie [verified: libsession.create() at line 6-7 builds the cookie as base64(json) with no HMAC or signature; libsession.load() blindly trusts the decoded JSON, and g.session['username'] from this forgeable cookie is used for all authorization checks across mod_posts, mod_user, and mod_mfa — any attacker can impersonate admin by base64-encoding {'username':'admin'}.]

Session forgery via unsigned base64-encoded JSON cookie — Complete identity spoofing, impersonate any user including admin, bypass all session-based access controls [verified: libsession.load() at line 20 calls json.loads(base64.b64decode(cookie)) with no cryptographic integrity check; the deserialized username is stored in g.session and trusted for all access-control decisions in mod_posts, mod_user, and mod_mfa, enabling trivial session forgery for any user.]

SQL Injection in login query — Authentication bypass, arbitrary data extraction from the database, potential data modification [verified: request.form username/password from mod_user.do_login() flows directly into libuser.login() which builds SQL via .format() string interpolation with no parameterization, escaping, or any sanitization — classic SQLi allowing authentication bypass.]

SQL Injection in user creation — Arbitrary SQL execution during user registration, data corruption, privilege escalation [verified: request.form username/password from mod_user.do_create() flows into libuser.create() which uses %-formatting to build an INSERT with attacker-supplied values — no parameterization or sanitization exists anywhere on the path.]

Passwords stored in plaintext without hashing — Complete exposure of all user passwords if the database is compromised; no brute-force resistance [verified: libuser.create() stores passwords verbatim via %s interpolation into the users table; libuser.login() compares the raw submitted password against the stored plaintext; db_init.py seeds initial users with plaintext passwords — no hashing exists anywhere in bad/.]

SQL Injection in password change via form and tampered session cookie — Arbitrary password overwrite for any user, privilege escalation [verified: Same UPDATE sink as finding [2]: password from request.form and username from an unsigned forgeable base64-encoded JSON cookie both reach .format()-built SQL in libuser.password_change() with zero sanitization on either input vector.]

Missing authentication check on password change route — Unauthenticated password change when combined with session forgery, allowing account takeover [verified: do_chpasswd() directly accesses g.session['username'] at line 80 with no 'username' not in g.session guard (unlike mod_mfa.py lines 17,38,60 and mod_posts.py lines 15,27); the session cookie is trivially forgeable — libsession.create() only base64-encodes raw JSON with no HMAC/signature — enabling an attacker to craft a cookie for any username and change that user's password.]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY in SSL variant — Session forgery; an attacker who knows the key can sign arbitrary Flask session cookies [verified: Line 13 hardcodes SECRET_KEY='aaaaaaa' with no override, environment variable, or key rotation; this weak static secret is used for Flask session signing, allowing an attacker who knows it to forge arbitrary session cookies and impersonate any user.]

Debug mode enabled in production SSL variant — Remote code execution via Werkzeug debugger; full server compromise [verified: Line 29 sets debug=True with no conditional guard (e.g., os.environ check), enabling the Werkzeug interactive debugger which exposes a PIN-protected console capable of arbitrary code execution on the server.]

API key glob injection in authentication — Authentication bypass via wildcard injection; attacker can match any API key and impersonate arbitrary users [verified: The X-APIKEY header flows unsanitized into Path.glob('vulpy.apikey.*.' + key) at line 33; sending '*' as the key matches all API key files and authenticates as the first matched user with no middleware or validation intercepting it.]

MFA secrets and user data exposed to logs via SQL trace callback — MFA secrets and usernames leaked to server logs, enabling account takeover by anyone with log access [verified: set_trace_callback(print) on lines 8/24/39/56/73 of bad/libmfa.py prints every SQL statement to stdout; mfa_reset_secret on line 75 executes UPDATE users SET mfa_secret=? with the TOTP seed as a bound parameter, so the raw MFA secret appears in stdout/logs, and it is called from reachable routes GET/POST /mfa/ (mod_mfa.py lines 23-24, 41) with no compensating control.]

Plaintext passwords logged via SQL trace callback — Passwords and other sensitive data exposed in application logs, accessible to anyone with log access [verified: conn.set_trace_callback(print) is set in libuser.login(), libuser.userlist(), libuser.password_change(), libposts.get_posts(), libposts.post(), and all libmfa functions, printing every SQL query — including SELECT statements with plaintext passwords — directly to stdout.]

Mass assignment allows posting as arbitrary user via API — An attacker with their own valid API key can impersonate any user (including admin) and create posts under that user's identity, undermining data integrity and enabling social engineering. [verified: data.update(request.get_json()) at line 44 blindly merges attacker-supplied JSON into data, overwriting the API-key-authenticated username because post_schema lacks additionalProperties: False; the overridden username is then passed directly to libposts.post, enabling post creation as any user.]

Missing authentication on API post listing endpoint — Unauthenticated access to all users' posts via the API, data exposure [verified: do_post_list (line 47) returns any user's posts via GET /api/post/<username> with zero authentication check; no API key, session, or decorator enforces access, and the before_request handler merely loads g.session without aborting unauthenticated requests.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing endpoints, MFA disable via GET — Forced MFA disable, forced password change, forged post creation, and other state-changing actions performed on behalf of victim [verified: No CSRF protection exists anywhere—no tokens in templates, no CSRF middleware, no SameSite cookie attribute in libsession.py—affecting all state-changing endpoints (login, create, chpasswd, post, MFA enable/disable) as verified across mod_user.py, mod_posts.py, and mod_mfa.py.]

MFA disable via GET request (CSRF-enabled state change) — Attackers can disable a victim's MFA protection via a single GET request, degrading account security [verified: GET /mfa/disable performs a state-changing DB UPDATE via libmfa.mfa_disable() with no CSRF token, no confirmation, and the session cookie lacks SameSite (libsession.py set_cookie has no samesite/httponly/secure attrs); an tag in bad/payloads/hello.html confirms the attack vector.]

Missing rate limiting on login and registration endpoints enabling brute-force attacks — Automated credential brute-forcing, account takeover via password guessing [verified: Neither POST /user/login (line 11) nor POST /user/create has any rate-limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA mechanism; utils/httpbrute.py is a dedicated brute-force CLI that submits rapid POST requests to the login URL with a password list and success-string detection, confirming the endpoint is trivially brute-forceable.]

Account enumeration and password oracle via MFA response differentiation — Credential validation oracle, targeted brute-force attacks against known-valid credentials [verified: Same differential response as finding [2]: do_login() returns 'Invalid user or password' for bad credentials vs 'Invalid OTP' when both username AND password are correct but MFA validation fails; an attacker who receives 'Invalid OTP' has definitively confirmed both the username and password, creating a full credential oracle.]

Hardcoded JWT signing secret enables API token forgery — Attacker can forge API tokens for any user, bypassing API authentication to read posts or perform actions via the REST API. [verified: good/libapi.py:11 hardcodes secret='MYSUPERSECRETKEY' which is used as the HMAC key in jwt.encode() for token signing (line 22) and jwt.decode() for verification (line 34); good/mod_api.py imports libapi and calls both keygen() and authenticate() on reachable /api/key and /api/post routes, making forged JWTs trivially craftable by any attacker who reads the source.]

Hardcoded Fernet encryption key enables session forgery — Attacker can forge session cookies to impersonate any user, including admin, gaining full access to all authenticated functionality. [verified: The Fernet key `'JHtM1wEt1I1J9N_Evjwqr3yYauXIqSxYzFnRhcf0ZG0='` is hardcoded at libsession.py:10 and used to encrypt/decrypt all session cookies via fernet.encrypt()/decrypt() in create() and load(); no external config or env-var overrides exist, so any source-code leak enables arbitrary session forgery.]

SQL query trace logging exposes sensitive data to logs — Sensitive data including usernames and MFA secrets is written to stdout/logs where it may be accessible to unauthorized operators or leaked through log aggregation systems. [verified: Every DB function in good/libuser.py, good/libposts.py, and good/libmfa.py calls conn.set_trace_callback(print), printing full SQL queries with bound parameters—including MFA TOTP seeds and password hashes—to stdout with no redaction or suppression.]

Missing Brute-Force Protection on API Key Generation Endpoint — Attackers can perform automated password guessing at high velocity via the API, potentially compromising user accounts and obtaining valid JWT tokens to access the authenticated API endpoints. [verified: The POST /api/key endpoint at mod_api.py:40 performs credential validation via libapi.keygen()/libuser.login() with no rate limiting, no account lockout, no incremental delay, and no Flask-Limiter or custom throttle anywhere in the codebase. The regex username pattern ^[a-z]+$ further simplifies automated brute-force enumeration.]

Unauthenticated Access to API Post Listing Endpoint — Unauthenticated attackers can read all post content for any and all users via the API, bypassing any intended access controls and exposing potentially sensitive user-generated content. [verified: The GET /api/post/<username> handler at mod_api.py:50-52 has zero authentication checks — no session validation, no API-key/JWT check, no call to libapi.authenticate() — and the app's before_request handler only deserializes the session without enforcing authentication. Any unauthenticated caller can enumerate and read all posts for any username.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint enables brute-force attacks — Attacker can brute-force user passwords through unlimited automated login attempts, compromising user accounts. [verified: No rate limiting, account lockout, or progressive delay exists on the /user/login POST handler (mod_user.py:12) or in libuser.login(); requirements.txt lists no rate-limiting library, and the httpbrute.py script in the repo confirms unlimited brute-force attempts succeed.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing endpoints — Attacker can force authenticated victims to change their password, create posts as the victim, enable/disable MFA, or perform any state-changing action by luring them to a malicious page. [verified: No CSRF tokens are generated or validated anywhere: mod_user.py, mod_mfa.py, mod_posts.py accept state-changing POSTs with only cookie-based session auth and no CSRF token check; the sole Referer guard on /mfa/disable (mod_mfa.py:58) checks for exact string 'vulpy.com', which is trivially bypassed by stripping the Referer header.]

Debug mode enabled in production SSL variant (good) — Remote code execution via Werkzeug debugger; full server compromise [verified: app.run(debug=True) at vulpy-ssl.py:29 enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger with RCE. While bound to 127.0.1.1 (localhost), this is a genuine CWE-489 misconfiguration reachable by local users or processes.]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY — Compromised SECRET_KEY enables forging of Flask-signed data and weakens any security mechanisms relying on it; source code exposure reveals the key. [verified: The SECRET_KEY '123aa8a93bdde342c871564a62282af857bda14b3359fde95d0c5e4b321610c1' is literally hardcoded at good/vulpy.py line 17 with no environment-variable override; it is committed to source and used by Flask for internal signing operations regardless of the custom Fernet session layer in libsession.py.]

Flask debug mode enabled with Werkzeug interactive debugger — An attacker who reaches the debugger console can execute arbitrary Python code on the server, leading to full system compromise. [verified: app.run(debug=True, ...) at good/vulpy.py line 53 enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger and detailed error tracebacks; although bound to loopback (127.0.1.1), the debug mode is a genuine production misconfiguration that leaks sensitive internals to any local client and exposes the /console debugger to local/SSRF-based attackers.]

Insecure PRNG used for API key generation enables key prediction — API key forgery; attacker can authenticate as any user via the API [verified: bad/libapi.py:14 uses random.getrandbits(2048) (Mersenne Twister, non-CSPRNG) for API key generation, reachable via POST /api/key; while the SHA-256 hashing of the raw PRNG output impedes direct state recovery from observed keys, the underlying entropy source is cryptographically weak for security-sensitive key material.]

Glob injection in API key deletion via crafted username — Denial of service via deletion of other users' API key files in /tmp/ [verified: bad/libapi.py:16 interpolates the username from the JSON request body directly into Path.glob('vulpy.apikey.' + username + '.*') with only JSON type validation (string), no content sanitization; since libuser.create() imposes no username constraints, an attacker can register a user named '*' and call POST /api/key to glob-match and unlink() all users' API key files in /tmp/, causing DoS via file d]

Session cookie missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags — Session cookies can be stolen via XSS (no HttpOnly), intercepted over non-HTTPS connections (no Secure), and sent in cross-site requests (no SameSite) [verified: response.set_cookie('vulpy_session', session) at libsession.py:7 omits httponly, secure, and samesite flags; no Flask app-level SESSION_COOKIE_* config overrides exist, so the cookie is transmitted without protection against XSS exfiltration, MITM interception, or cross-site request forgery.]

Password complexity check is a no-op stub — Users can set trivially weak passwords (e.g., 'a', '123') enabling rapid brute-force compromise [verified: password_complexity() unconditionally returns True in libuser.py:60, making the check in do_chpasswd() a dead no-op; do_create() never even calls it — there is zero password strength enforcement anywhere in the application.]

IDOR - Insecure Direct Object Reference on post viewing — Unauthorized access to any user's private posts, user enumeration, data leakage [verified: When a username is provided in the URL path, do_view() passes it directly to libposts.get_posts(username) with no authentication or authorization check; the session-based username fallback is only used when no URL username is supplied, so any anonymous user can enumerate and read any user's posts.]

Missing CSRF protection on post creation endpoint — Cross-site request forgery: attacker can force authenticated users to create posts without their knowledge [verified: POST /posts/ at bad/mod_posts.py:25 creates posts using only cookie-based auth (g.session['username']) with no CSRF token in the form (bad/templates/posts.view.html) or handler, no Flask-WTF/middleware in vulpy.py, and no SameSite attribute on the session cookie in libsession.py — a cross-site form can silently force authenticated users to create posts.]

User enumeration via differential login error messages — Attackers can enumerate valid credentials by distinguishing between invalid login and valid login with MFA required [verified: do_login() returns flash('Invalid user or password') on bad credentials (line 22) but flash('Invalid OTP') when credentials are correct and MFA is enabled but OTP is missing/wrong (line 25); an attacker observing the error message change from the first to the second confirms a valid username/password pair.]

Missing rate limiting on user registration endpoint — Automated bulk account creation; resource exhaustion; spam user generation [verified: The /user/create endpoint accepts POST with username/password and calls libuser.create() with zero rate-limiting, CAPTCHA, or throttling — no Flask-Limiter, decorator, or brute-force guard exists anywhere in bad/.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing routes — Attackers can force authenticated users to change passwords, create posts, enable/disable MFA, or perform other actions without their knowledge [verified: No CSRF tokens exist in any POST form templates; libsession.create() sets the vulpy_session cookie via response.set_cookie() with no SameSite attribute; no @before_request CSRF check, Origin/Referer validation, or Flask-WTF integration exists anywhere in bad/. The app binds to 127.0.1.1:5000 (localhost) limiting remote exploitation, but a local attacker can still force state-changing actions on an]

Hardcoded weak Flask SECRET_KEY — Session forgery if Flask signed sessions are enabled, enables other cryptographic attacks on Flask internals [verified: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'aaaaaaa' is hardcoded at bad/vulpy.py:12; the custom libsession (unsigned base64 JSON cookies) does not rely on it, but a known secret weakens any Flask internals or extensions that do.]

Sensitive data exposed to logs via SQL trace callback (good variant) — Post content and user data leaked to server logs [verified: conn.set_trace_callback(print) at lines 10 and 22 logs every SQL query with bound parameters (usernames, post text) to stdout with no filtering or redirection, and these functions are reachable via Flask routes GET /posts/<username> and POST /posts/ in mod_posts.py.]

Session cookie missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags — Session cookie can be stolen via XSS (no HttpOnly), intercepted over unencrypted connections (no Secure), and sent on cross-site requests (no SameSite), enabling session hijacking. [verified: response.set_cookie('vulpy_session',...) at libsession.py:32 and :60 omits httponly=True (JS-readable cookie, enabling theft via any XSS) and samesite=... (enables CSRF with no anti-CSRF tokens present anywhere in the app); the existing CSP nonce mitigates some XSS vectors but does not substitute for HttpOnly cookie protection.]

User enumeration via timing side-channel in login — Attacker can enumerate valid usernames by measuring login response times, building a target list for credential-stuffing or password-spraying attacks. [verified: login() in good/libuser.py returns False immediately at line 22 for non-existent users but runs slow Scrypt KDF verify (n=2^14) at line 35 for existing users, with no dummy computation or constant-time delay to mask the timing difference.]

IDOR — insecure direct object reference on post viewing (good variant) — Unauthorized access to any user's private post content [verified: The /posts/<username> route at good/mod_posts.py:15 takes a username from the URL path and passes it directly to libposts.get_posts() with no ownership or authorization check — any user (authenticated or not) can view any other user's posts. No decorator, middleware, or code-level guard restricts access.]

Missing CSRF protection on post creation (good variant) — CSRF: attacker forces authenticated users to create posts without consent [verified: The POST /posts/ handler at good/mod_posts.py:25 creates posts using only session-cookie auth with no CSRF token in the form (posts.view.html) or in the route handler. No CSRF middleware, Flask-WTF, or any anti-CSRF mechanism exists anywhere in the good codebase; the referer check in mod_mfa.py protects only the MFA-disable endpoint.]

Missing rate limiting on secondary login/create endpoint (good variant) — Brute-force password guessing via the unrated secondary authentication endpoint [verified: The /user/create endpoint at good/mod_user.py:39 calls libuser.login() for authentication but has no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection — none exist anywhere in the good/ codebase — creating an unrestricted secondary login endpoint for password guessing.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production — Arbitrary code execution on the server via Werkzeug debugger console if an exception is triggered [verified: app.run(debug=True) at bad/vulpy.py:41 enables the Werkzeug debugger; binding to 127.0.1.1 limits exposure to localhost and the PIN provides some protection, but an unhandled exception still exposes an interactive console on the loopback interface.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production — Remote code execution via Werkzeug debugger console when an exception is triggered [verified: app.run(debug=True) at bad/vulpy.py:41 enables the Werkzeug debugger; binding to 127.0.1.1 limits exposure to localhost and the PIN provides some protection, but an unhandled exception still exposes an interactive console on the loopback interface.]
